newsitem.title: USA: Dollar drifts at weaker levels at U.S. open.
newsitem.headline: Dollar drifts at weaker levels at U.S. open.

text.p: The dollar opened weaker against the mark as traders mulled over talk about a possible delay in European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and the latest comments from German officials about plans to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves, currency experts said.
Chris Turner, a research director at I.D.E.A. Inc, said there were rumors going around about a one-year delay in EMU this morning.
Turner attributed the EMU delay talk to "just people trying to work out how this issue is going to be resolved."
After the meeting between Tietmeyer and Waigel, coalition sources told reporters "the result will have an effect from 1997 to 1998, and in that way we are coming to an agreed solution."
Mike Malpede, a senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd, said the announcement is probably not overly constructive for dollar/mark and doubted that it would have a big impact.
Indeed the dollar continued to trade in a fairly narrow range versus the mark after the news from Bonn hit the market.

EMU is slated to start on January 1, 1999. A victory by the left in French general elections this weekend and Bonn's plan to revalue Buba's gold reserves has left foreign exchange markets speculating about the future of EMU.
Shortly before the opening, the dollar slid towards 1.7220 marks in the U.S. then bounced off the bottom to open at 1.7258/63 marks, still lower than 1.7290/00 at Monday's close.
John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank, said, "Some people walking in the door in New York (saw) the dollar at lower levels ... and just decided to take advantage of it."

Both Buba President Hans Tietmeyer and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel emerged from a meeting on Tuesday with upbeat comments about hopes for an agreement on government plans to revalue Buba's assets.
Bill Bertha, chief dealer at Mellon Bank N.A., said anticipation that the two might be drawing closer to an agreement on the revaluation plan had helped the mark.
After the opening, Reuters reported that Bonn coalition sources revealed the government will get profits from revaluation of Buba gold reserves in 1998.
Meanwhile, the dollar managed to climbed above 116 yen after opening at 115.87/97 yen. It had closed at 116.55/65 yen on Monday.
Dollar/yen was helped by dollar gains against the Swiss franc and mark, according to Doug Lee, an assistant vice president at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York.
However, Lee said he expected the dollar to trade between 115.50 yen and 116.50 yen for the next few days until it breaks higher.
The dollar rose to 1.4325/35 Swiss francs at the open from 1.4320/30 francs at the close and then climbed further.
Elsewhere, sterling opened little changed at $1.6360/70 versus $1.6362/72.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3724/29 from C$1.3737/42.
The Australian dollar opened at $0.7575/80 compared with $0.7567/72.
